**Problem 10 (Challenge): How long until a research breakthrough pays off?** Suppose that AI tools make researchers twice as productive from 2050 on (a hypothetical scenario): in the Romer model of Fig. 3, $\bar{z}$ rises from 1 to 2, with $\gamma = 0.6$ and $\bar{n} = 0.05$.

(a) Set $\bar{z}' = 2$ with the slider. What is the long-run level effect, and how fast does output per person grow in 2051?

(b) Let $x_t \equiv A_t/A_t^*$ be the stock of ideas relative to its new BGP value. Use the production of ideas and equation (3) to show that $x_{t+1} = (x_t + \bar{n})/(1+\bar{n})$, so that the gap $1 - x_t$ shrinks by the factor $1/(1+\bar{n})$ every year.

(c) How many years does it take to close half of the gap in ideas? Does the answer depend on $\bar{z}'$ or $\gamma$?

(d) In which year is output per person within 10 percent of its new BGP when $\bar{z}' = 2$, and when $\bar{z}' = 8$? Use $y_t/y_t^* = x_t^{\gamma}$, then confirm with `simulate_romer`.

(e) A politician promises that the gains from AI will arrive within a decade. Is that right?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For (b), write the production of ideas as $A_{t+1} = A_t + \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t$, note from equation (3) that $\bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t = \bar{n}A_t^*$ and $A_{t+1}^* = (1+\bar{n})A_t^*$, and divide. In 2050 the stock of ideas has not moved yet, so $x_{2050} = \bar{z}/\bar{z}'$. For (d), solve $x_t^{0.6} \geq 0.9$ for the gap $1 - x_t$.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(rise_in_z,
         z_new=FloatSlider(value=4.0, min=1.5, max=10.0, step=0.5, description="new research productivity z̄'", style=WIDE),
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["ratio", "linear"], description="vertical scale"));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 3 above, adapted from Fig. 6.3 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The title reads "New BGP ×1.52 the old | growth 5.9% in 2051, 3.1% in 2100 (BGP: 3.0%)". The new BGP is $2^{0.6} \approx 1.52$ times the old one (equation 4), and output per person grows by 5.9 percent in 2051: by equation (6), ideas grow by $0.05\times2 = 10$ percent in that first year, and $1.10^{0.6} - 1 \approx 5.9$ percent.

**(b)** From equation (3), $A_t^* = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/\bar{n}$, so the yearly flow of new ideas is $\bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t = \bar{n}A_t^*$, and $A_t^*$ grows with $N_t$: $A_{t+1}^* = (1+\bar{n})A_t^*$. Then

$$x_{t+1} = \frac{A_{t+1}}{A_{t+1}^*} = \frac{A_t + \bar{n}A_t^*}{(1+\bar{n})A_t^*} = \frac{x_t + \bar{n}}{1+\bar{n}},$$

$$1 - x_{t+1} = \frac{1 + \bar{n} - x_t - \bar{n}}{1+\bar{n}} = \frac{1 - x_t}{1+\bar{n}}.$$

The gap between the stock of ideas and its BGP value shrinks by the same factor, $1/1.05 \approx 0.952$, every year.

**(c)** After $T$ years the gap is $(1-x_{2050})/(1+\bar{n})^T$. Half of it is closed when $(1+\bar{n})^T = 2$, that is after

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{n})} = \frac{0.693}{0.0488} \approx 14.2 \text{ years},$$

so by 2065. Neither $\bar{z}'$ nor $\gamma$ appears: the speed at which the gap in ideas closes depends only on $\bar{n}$, the growth of the research workforce.

**(d)** Output per person is within 10 percent of its new BGP when $x_t^{0.6} \geq 0.9$, that is $x_t \geq 0.9^{1/0.6} = 0.839$, or a gap $1 - x_t \leq 0.161$. With $\bar{z}' = 2$, $x_{2050} = 1/2$ and the gap starts at 0.5, so we need $1.05^T \geq 0.5/0.161$, $T \geq 23.2$: the year **2074**. With $\bar{z}' = 8$, the gap starts at $1 - 1/8 = 0.875$, so $T \geq 34.7$: the year **2085**.

```python
for z_new in [2.0, 8.0]:
    years, y, y_bgp = simulate_romer(z_new=z_new)
    close = years[(years >= 2050) & (y >= 0.9 * y_bgp)]      # within 10% of the new BGP
    print(f"z' = {z_new}: within 10% of the new BGP from {close[0]}")
print(f"Half-life of the gap in ideas: {np.log(2) / np.log(1.05):.1f} years")
```

**(e)** No. With $\bar{z}' = 2$, after ten years the gap in ideas is still $0.5/1.05^{10} = 0.307$, so output per person is $0.693^{0.6} \approx 0.80$ times its new BGP: about 42 percent of the long-run gain has arrived (output is 1.22 times the old path, out of an eventual 1.52). Because the gap closes by only $1 - 1/1.05$, less than 5 percent, each year whatever the size of the boost, the full gains of a better research technology take decades, not years.

</details>
